paras: The Macon lynch crowds of January 1903 gathered in Macon, Georgia, after Thomas J. Conrad, a baggage agent at the Union depot, was shot and killed on January 5, and a young Black employee, Oscar Shiver, was accused of the shooting. A crowd shouted threats at Shiver's arrested brother, and crowds later assembled to take a Black man arrested on a train from officers and lynch him. The man proved not to be Shiver, no prisoner was brought back, and no one was killed.

According to the Savannah Morning News correspondent at Macon, Conrad was shot at about 8:30 on the morning of January 5 after a dispute a few hours earlier over the young man's coming to work late on Sunday. A shorter wire version named the accused Arthur Shiver, a wagon driver, and said the trouble arose over some baggage. Shiver ran for the swamp, and Sheriff Wescott and a posse took up his trail.

His brother, Jim Shiver, was arrested, and a coroner's jury declared him an accomplice on testimony that he had made a remark about Conrad on Saturday night. The Associated Press reported that as Jim Shiver was put into the patrol wagon, a large crowd shouted, "if you were the right man you would never be allowed to get in that wagon." The Savannah correspondent wrote that "many" said Shiver would never be put in jail if caught, while the authorities were taking "every precaution against violence."

On a night the report does not date, a Black man boarded the southbound Southern train in the Macon yards and rode to Bullards, where Conductor John A. Eldson pulled him from the coach. Baggagemaster Marion Baughan, a former Macon detective, thought he answered the description, and the sheriff at Eastman met the train and took him into custody. When officers from Macon arrived, they found he was not Shiver. In the paper's words, "Crowds gathered at Macon to take the negro from the officers and lynch him, but they had no prisoner on their return."

Governor Terrell offered a $150 reward for Arthur Shivers, wanted for Conrad's murder on January 5. In March a Macon detective went to St. Augustine, Florida, for a prisoner believed to be Shivers, a man who had been beaten by several officers when arrested there. No report of a capture, trial, or further mob action was found, and no arrests of anyone in the crowds were reported.

White papers reported the killing widely as a wire item, under headlines such as "NEGRO KILLED CONRAD" in Savannah and "Negro Kills Man" in Americus. The Associated Press version, carried in Raleigh and in Newberry, South Carolina, framed the crowd's threat as public feeling, describing excitement as "intense" and indignation as "openly expressed." News digests in Bamberg, South Carolina, and Palatka, Florida, mentioned only the killing and the escape.

The lynch crowds themselves appeared only in the Savannah Morning News, as the last sentence of a January 8 story headlined "WASN'T THE MURDERER," without comment. The same paper described Conrad as "genial, accommodating and liked by everybody" and said the killing appeared planned "in cold blood." No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The papers differed on the accused's first name, with Oscar in the Macon and Associated Press reports and Arthur in a shorter wire and the governor's reward notice. They also differed on the cause of the quarrel, lateness or baggage, and on whether Conrad died instantly or twenty minutes later; the fuller Macon account gives the lateness dispute and the twenty minutes.

reader.title: Macon lynch crowds after the killing of Thomas J. Conrad
bases: After a Black employee was accused of shooting baggage agent Thomas J. Conrad, a crowd shouted threats at his arrested brother (A5) and crowds gathered at Macon to take a suspect from officers and lynch him; no one was killed (A8).

Crowds gathered to take a suspect from officers and lynch him over Conrad's killing, an illegal group act under a pretext of justice, but the officers returned without a prisoner and no one was killed (A8); this was a threatened lynching.

The Savannah Morning News reports talk that Shiver would never be jailed (A4) and the lynch crowds awaiting the train suspect (A8), and the Associated Press independently reports a threatening crowd at Jim Shiver's arrest (A5, A11); the train-suspect crowd itself appears only in A8.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News Macon correspondent
accounts.gist: Shiver shot Conrad over a trifling dispute about coming to work late, apparently planned 'in cold blood'; many said he would never be put in jail if caught; later, crowds gathered to lynch a suspect who proved to be the wrong man.

accounts.label: Associated Press
accounts.gist: Shiver killed Conrad over lateness; excitement was intense and a large crowd shouted at Jim Shiver that the right man would never reach the patrol wagon.

accounts.label: Wire brief (other version)
accounts.gist: Arthur Shiver, a wagon driver, shot Conrad, manager of the Macon Baggage Transfer company, over a dispute about baggage; Conrad died instantly.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News called Conrad 'genial' and 'liked by everybody', reported that 'many' said Shiver would never be jailed, and noted the lynch crowds in one closing sentence without comment.
The AP story, headlined 'People Indignant Because Negro Shot Him Over Trifling Dispute', presented the crowd's threat as public indignation.
Digests in South Carolina and Florida reported only the killing and the escape, with no crowd.

conflicts.note: The Macon correspondent and the AP use Oscar; a shorter wire and the governor's reward use Arthur.

conflicts.note: The fuller Macon and AP reports give the lateness dispute.

record_check.dossier: Shooting and crowd at the patrol wagon on Monday, January 5, 1903; train arrest and lynch crowds on an undated night between January 5 and 8. The January 3 date belongs to the messenger-boy strike (A2).
An unnamed Black man taken off the train (target of the crowds); Jim Shiver, the arrested brother, also threatened by a crowd.

record_check.record: said to have shot Baggagemaster Thomas J. Conrad
record_check.dossier: Accused of shooting and killing Conrad; the man threatened at Macon was not the accused; Jim Shiver was held as an accomplice.
Threat by crowds (a mob); no work action. 'work_action' and 'workers' come from the separate Western Union messenger dispute.
1 (Conrad, in the shooting that prompted the threat).
At least 13 white items in 8 papers on the killing and its sequel; the lynch crowd itself in one Savannah item; no Black-press coverage found.

info: Conrad was shot on the morning of Monday, January 5, 1903; the crowd shouted at Jim Shiver's arrest the same day; the train arrest and the lynch crowds followed on an undated night before January 8.
Union depot, Macon; the suspect was taken off a train at Bullards and handed to the sheriff at Eastman.

Targets of the crowds: an unnamed negro man taken off the southbound Southern train, found not to be Shivers (A8); Jim Shiver, arrested as an accomplice, at whom a crowd shouted (A5); Oscar Shiver, sought (A4).
Oscar (or Arthur) Shiver was accused of shooting and killing Thomas J. Conrad; Jim Shiver was held as an accomplice.
Unnamed 'crowds' at Macon; a 'large crowd' at the patrol wagon. Race not stated.
No one was lynched; Oscar Shiver remained at large into March 1903.

set_aside: Western Union messenger boys strike at Macon over a pay cut; manager says he may hire negroes. Labor dispute only.
Fourteen negroes replace striking white messenger boys at Macon; 'The white boys declare that they will mob the negroes.' Separate labor threat, not the Conrad case.
Macon patrons petition Western Union to discharge negro messengers; no violence.
Rufus Shivers, a different man, shot and captured by a posse at Sparta.
